To say the model decided is to give a role's responsibility to something that holds no role, and the people who do hold it slip out from under it. Responsibility in a role cannot be handed to something that holds no role. A loan officer who says the model decided is still the loan officer; the misnaming lets her stop acting as one.

The practical cost of the word is in the relationships. People told that a system decided about them have no one to hold to what the position owes them, and that leaves the relationship between institution and person empty. A teacher tells a parent the grading software decided the mark. The parent wants to talk to the teacher, whose job it was.

A Utilitarian will object that whether we call it a decision changes nothing about what the output does to people, so the dispute is about words while the harms are real. Words are not idle here. What we call the act decides whom we hold to account for it, and harms that no one is held to account for are harms that go on. Correct naming is the start of correct conduct, and here it points every question back to the office that put the model to work.

The word decide does work the system has not done, which makes this a mistake that matters: getting the name right keeps responsibility with the people whose roles the decision belongs to. The practical cost of the word is in the relationships. People told that a system decided about them have no one to hold to what the position owes them, and that leaves the relationship between institution and person empty.

Responsibility in a role cannot be handed to something that holds no role. A loan officer who says the model decided is still the loan officer; the misnaming lets her stop acting as one. A bank tells a customer that the system decided to refuse her. The customer asks to speak to whoever decided, and there is no such person on the list.

A decision is something a person in a role owes others, and the model holds no role to owe it from.

Calling the output a decision lets the officer, the manager and the clinician speak as if they had not decided, which is the real harm. Book 13 warns that when names are not correct, what is said stops matching how things are, and nothing that rests on it can be done well. Calling an output a decision is such a case: it names an act of someone answerable, when no one answerable has acted.

The practical cost of the word is in the relationships. People told that a system decided about them have no one to hold to what the position owes them, and that leaves the relationship between institution and person empty. A hospital manager says the scheduling model decided to cancel the operation. The surgeon who signed off on it is not mentioned.

An Ubuntu Ethicist will object that insisting the decision belongs to whoever holds the position keeps responsibility in a chain of command, when the people affected should also have a say in the decision. Holding the position to account is the first step to giving the affected a say, since there is then someone to answer them. A decision credited to a model has no one to answer anybody. Correct naming is the start of correct conduct, and here it points every question back to the office that put the model to work.

A Confucian accepts this as a case of incorrect names: decide names an act by someone in a position, and the model occupies no position. Decisions belong to positions. A judge decides, a doctor decides, a manager decides, and each answers to the people their role serves. A model produces text that someone in such a position then adopts, and the deciding was theirs.
